newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Canada sees trade missions as cure for jobless ills.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canada sees trade missions as cure for jobless ills.

text.p: When Canada's Prime Minister Jean Chretien goes abroad, he always remembers to pick up a few billion dollars' worth of souvenirs for the folks back home.
A contract here, a mega-deal there. There's usually room in the Chretien backpack for the goodies that win friends and influence elections.

Last week, the 62-year-old Canadian leader announced that on January 8 he would lead a high-powered delegation of politicians and business leaders to South Korea, the Philippines and Thailand on yet another international trade junket.
The trip will mark the third time in his three-year mandate that the self-professed "little guy" from Shawinigan, Quebec, has gone off to meet the big guys in Asia.

"They (Canadian firms) specialise in providing goods and services that help economies grow," Chretien said. "Sharing this know-how will ultimately benefit both ourselves and our Asia-Pacific partners."

In 1994 Chretien steered a 300-person delegation -- at the time the largest in Canadian history -- to China where gleeful Canadian business leaders fell over themselves to sign C$8.6 billion (US$6.33 billion) in contracts and "agreements".
The Canadian prime minister followed up the now-famous China tour with an equally lucrative cattle run to India, Pakistan, Malaysia, and Indonesia last year.
DO THE DEALS BREED JOBS?
"Jobs, jobs, jobs," Chretien answers when asked what these so-called "Team Canada" missions accomplish.

The Canadian government estimates 11,000 jobs are created for every C$1 billion (US$736.1 million) of Canadian exports. Government officials cannot, however, say what proportion of these trade deals involve Canadian exports.
The impression, in no way dissuaded by a political pro like Chretien, is that the entire C$17.2 billion (US$12.66 billion) in Asian contracts is entering the Canadian economy directly.
If true, the two recent Asian trips should have translated into about 200,000 new jobs for Canadians -- a suggestion openly mocked by trade experts.
Chretien claims his government has created 600,000 new jobs this year, but Canada's unemployment rate remains stalled at 10 percent.

"Where are all these new jobs?" asked John Crispo, a professor of political economy at the University of Toronto. "Two hundred thousand new jobs! That kind of jargon is ridiculous. We're getting far more jobs from our burgeoning trade with the United States."
CONTRACT BILLIONS MAY LACK BOUNCE
Crispo, a strong supporter of international trade, said Chretien should practise more trade and less politics on future trips.

"What bothers me is the politics of taking credit for what the private sector is doing," Crispo said. "A lot of what happens really is the private sector doing its job and the government being there to capitalise with some signatures."brought home by Chretien have less bounce than advertised.

Only C$2.6 billion (US$1.91 billion) in deals signed on last year's Southeast Asian trip appears solid. The remaining C$6 billion (US$4.41 billion) is in the form of agreements-in-principle whose future is uncertain.
More worrisome to Crispo is Canada's propensity to underwrite through its export credit agency, the Export Development Corporation, some of these trade deals.
One such deal includes the financing for two Canadian-made Candu nuclear reactors sold to China in 1994.
The idea of using C$1.5 billion (US$1.1 billion) of taxpayers' money to finance the sale of Candu reactors strains economic commmon sense, Crispo said.
HUMAN RIGHTS ON THE BACK BURNER
Besides attacks from the right, Chretien is also assailed by the left, which sees a darker thread running through the fabric of Canadian trade policy.

Human rights activists note that Canada's gracious hosts on previous trade missions have included Indonesia's President Suharto and China's Premier Li Peng -- both leaders with dubious human rights records.

"This push for (economic) liberalisation without ensuring that basic rights, like the rights of workers, are guaranteed is going to be very detrimental to the development of democracy in those countries," said Carole Samdup, a spokesperson for the Montreal-based International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development.
When pressed in Indonesia last year as to why his government would not push Asia on human rights issues, Chretien shot back "We're not running the government here".
Canada's willingness to shunt social issues aside in favour of all things economic leaves human rights activists perplexed.
The argument that the West must show patience with developing nations in human rights is shortsighted, Samdup said.
Canada's human rights record, however, is not the only one under the microscope.

Human Rights Watch slammed the United States, Japan and the European Union in its 1997 report for claiming that their trade and political policies would bolster human rights in countries like China and Russia.
